title: The One With The Ultimate Fighting Champ

jokes.text: Do you think there's a town in Missouri called Sample? And as you're driving into the town, there's a sign that says: 'You're in Sample.'
jokes.setup: A man muses about a hypothetical town named 'Sample' in Missouri.
jokes.punchline: 'You're in Sample' — the town's welcome sign doubles as the exact phrasing used on product samples, making the mundane name absurdly funny as a sign.
jokes.explanation: A clever wordplay observation that works on its own terms — the joke lands on the double meaning of 'You're in Sample.' Functional comedy that sets a casual tone but has no character integration since this is a stranger we never see again.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what I don't get? There's a town called Sample. Sample! And they probably have a sign that's just like, 'Welcome to Sample.' I mean, what else would it be? 'Welcome to Example'? No! It's Sample!

jokes.text: Monica starts telling her friends about Pete, gets interrupted by strangers crowding the booth asking everyone to 'scooch.'
jokes.setup: Monica's friends eagerly lean in to hear her big news about Pete.
jokes.punchline: Strangers interrupt repeatedly asking everyone to scoot over, completely derailing the moment.
jokes.explanation: Classic situational comedy — the group's anticipation is repeatedly undercut by mundane interruption. Works as a sustained bit but the 'scooch' gag is familiar territory.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Everyone just skooch over a little bit.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm skooching! I'm skooching as much as I can skooch!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well skooch more!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: There is no more skooch! I have skooched to my maximum skooch capacity!

jokes.text: Stranger confesses to his friend that he thinks his wife is sleeping with her gynecologist. 'He's got access. I know. It's a feeling you get.'
jokes.setup: A man at the diner confides he suspects his wife is sleeping with her gynecologist.
jokes.punchline: 'He's got access. I know.' Delivered with matter-of-fact resignation.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan 'He's got access' is genuinely funny — dark subject matter delivered with sad, clinical logic. Economy is strong; the line gets its laugh from understatement.

dialogue.speaker: Tim
dialogue.line: It's like wearing someone else's bowling shoes. You know something's off, but you can't quite put your finger on why. They fit okay, but they don't feel right. And you keep wondering... who wore these before me?

jokes.text: 'Like when you're in somebody else's bowling shoes?' / 'That's the one.'
jokes.setup: The man says knowing your wife is cheating is 'a feeling you get.'
jokes.punchline: Joey equates that specific emotional dread to wearing someone else's bowling shoes, and the stranger earnestly agrees.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent economy comedy — Joey's specific, absurd analogy (bowling shoes) for marital betrayal is both perfectly character-specific (Joey as the lovable simpleton) and unexpectedly resonant. The stranger's earnest confirmation 'That's the one' elevates it further, making the absurd feel profound. Strong character integration — this is quintessentially a Joey line.

dialogue.line: The gross revelation that it's still oozing

jokes.text: The man's wound is 'oozing' and he asks for cream to be passed at the diner table during this emotional confession.
jokes.setup: A man is emotionally unraveling about his wife's infidelity.
jokes.punchline: He has an oozing wound and casually asks for cream to treat it at the restaurant table mid-confession.
jokes.explanation: Gross-out discomfort comedy that works primarily because of the contrast — emotional vulnerability mixed with bodily grossness. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tim
dialogue.line: I think my wife is cheating on me with her gynecologist.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: That's terrible. I'm so sorry to hear that.

dialogue.speaker: Tim
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've been suspicious for weeks. She's always going to her appointments, and she comes back looking so... satisfied.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Well, have you confronted her about it?

dialogue.speaker: Tim
dialogue.line: I'm about to. I'm going to demand to know who this gynecologist is.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Tim... it's me. I'm her gynecologist.

jokes.text: The man confesses to Tomas: 'I've been sleeping with your wife.' / 'You're the gynecologist?'
jokes.setup: The man solemnly confesses to his friend Tomas that he's been sleeping with his wife — an apparently devastating revelation.
jokes.punchline: Tomas's response ('You're the gynecologist?') reveals the betrayal is a layer deeper — he already suspected the gynecologist and now discovers this friend is the same man.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed callback that ties together two earlier setups (the gynecologist suspicion AND the confession). The structure is tight: 'You're the gynecologist?' works as both a reveal and a punchline. Strong economy, and the misdirection — we think the confession is the main event, but the real joke is the Tomas reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I had this whole thing prepared, and I was going to come in here and tell you exactly how I felt, and I was so angry, and I had all these things written down...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And I completely forgot what I was going to say.

jokes.text: Monica attempts to share her Pete news; strangers keep interrupting asking for napkins and items, derailing the conversation entirely.
jokes.setup: Monica keeps trying to tell her friends about Pete amid the stranger chaos.
jokes.punchline: Each attempt is thwarted by increasingly mundane stranger requests (napkins, items), making the interruption itself the escalating joke.
jokes.explanation: The running interruption gag is serviceable but stretched thin by this third beat. The comedic return diminishes with each repetition without a satisfying escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know, if you're gonna get married, you should really think about changing your last name. I mean, 'Monica Geller' — it's not terrible, but 'Monica Bing'? That's a whole new thing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I like my name.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, that's good, because you're keeping it.

jokes.text: The strangers' argument escalates dramatically — 'We are finished! Nada! No more! You are a bastard!' — then 'Come back!'
jokes.setup: The strangers' dispute has been building; the man delivers a furious, definitive break.
jokes.punchline: 'Come back!' immediately after 'Stay away from me!' deflates all the dramatic posturing.
jokes.explanation: The 'Come back!' punchline is a reliable comedic structure — big dramatic declaration immediately undercut by neediness. Works well and lands, but it's a familiar comedic move.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, so in Ultimate Fighting, it's anything goes?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, pretty much. You can do almost anything.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Almost? What can't you do?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you can't bite, you can't pull hair, you can't strike the groin...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So it's not really 'anything goes' then, is it?

jokes.text: 'So, what were you gonna tell us?' / 'I have no idea.'
jokes.setup: After the entire diner chaos, Monica's friends finally get a quiet moment and circle back to ask what her news was.
jokes.punchline: Monica has completely forgotten what she was going to say.
jokes.explanation: Clean button on the whole opening sequence. The payoff to all the interruption chaos is Monica having completely lost her train of thought — a satisfying structural close. Economy is excellent; the joke needs exactly four words to land.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh thank God, I was dreading having to explain that.

jokes.text: 'Or should I say, Mrs. Monica Becker?' / 'Oh, keep your name. Don't take his name.' / 'He didn't ask me to marry him.' / 'Then definitely don't take his name!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe teases Monica about Pete possibly proposing, saying 'Mrs. Monica Becker?'
jokes.punchline: When Monica says he didn't propose, the friend immediately reverses her advice with 'Then definitely don't take his name!' — the reversal is fast and confident.
jokes.explanation: Tight, well-structured flip. The advice-reversal joke lands because of delivery speed and the absurd formality of someone advising on name changes when no proposal happened. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I washed my hands in duck water.

dialogue.speaker: Other
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because I bathed a duck in the sink!

jokes.text: Monica describing Ultimate Fighting: 'It's sort of like wrestling. But without the costumes. And it's not fake. It's totally brutal. Two guys in the ring and the rules are, there are no rules!'
jokes.setup: Monica is explaining Ultimate Fighting to her friends.
jokes.punchline: Her description as 'sort of like wrestling but without the costumes' and 'the rules are there are no rules' — she's explaining this with earnest, breathless severity.
jokes.explanation: Monica's naive sincerity in explaining something she barely understands is the joke. Functional character comedy but not a standout moment — the 'no rules' line is a cliché of the genre being mocked.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: You know, it doesn't matter if you fail. What matters is that you tried.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great, Doug. Although I have to say, that's the same thing my gym instructor told me, and I'm pretty sure he was just trying to make me feel better about passing out on the treadmill.

jokes.text: 'I heard you made a great 12-year-old.' / 'It was the best year of my life.'
jokes.setup: Chandler makes a dig at Joey, presumably referencing an acting role where Joey played a 12-year-old.
jokes.punchline: Joey responds with complete earnestness — 'It was the best year of my life' — taking the insult as a compliment and reminiscing fondly.
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration — Joey's oblivious pride in having played a child is perfectly in character. The deadpan nostalgia ('it was the best year of my life') reframes the insult as a fond memory, which is funnier than any comeback would be. This is a well-executed character comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm worried about making jokes at work. What if my boss doesn't think I'm funny?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I told him one of my jokes today and he loved it. He's promoting me!

jokes.text: 'What's fish-hooking?' / [someone demonstrates with their fingers] / 'Thanks. That would have been hard to describe.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks what 'fish-hooking' is (a brutal fighting move).
jokes.punchline: Someone demonstrates physically (hooking a finger into a mouth/nose), and the response — 'Thanks, that would have been hard to describe' — acknowledges how grotesque and yet efficient the demonstration was.
jokes.explanation: Mostly a visual gag with a strong verbal button. The transcript can't capture the physical demonstration but the response line 'That would have been hard to describe' is a clean deadpan that gets good mileage from the visual. Rewatch value because the physical bit is presumably funny on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't say anything to her about it. What if she takes it the wrong way?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler, she's sexually harassing you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, but what if I say something and she gets mad and then she doesn't sexually harass me anymore? Then I'll have gotten mad for nothing!

jokes.text: 'My hands are totally clean. I just gave the duck a bath.'
jokes.setup: Someone has apparently tasted something unpleasant after Joey demonstrated the fish-hook (or was touched by him).
jokes.punchline: Joey's defense is that his hands are clean because he just bathed the duck — which is both reassuring and deeply not reassuring.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the absurdity of having a pet duck, and the fact that 'I just gave the duck a bath' is both an explanation and an escalation of the grossness concern. Strong character integration — Joey having a duck is show lore, and his genuine belief that this is reassuring is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's like if someone came up to you and just started touching your butt. You wouldn't be okay with that, would you?

jokes.text: 'There is no I in team.' / 'Yes, but there's two in martini. So, everybody, back to my office.'
jokes.setup: Doug gives the classic motivational speech: 'There is no I in team.'
jokes.punchline: 'Yes, but there's two in martini' — subverting the motivational cliché to justify day drinking, delivered with complete authority.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely quotable joke with clean structure. The wordplay on 'martini' having two I's is a clever subversion of a tired motivational cliché, and the immediate pivot to 'back to my office' makes Doug an instantly vivid comic character. High quotability — this line lives outside the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! If you're gonna grab her boob, you gotta be gentle about it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying, you can't just go in there like you're trying to find the last good grape in the bunch.

jokes.text: Doug calls Chandler 'Chuckles' and then demands his name; Chandler says 'Bing' apologetically. Doug responds: 'Funny. I like funny.'
jokes.setup: Chandler makes a witty remark at the work meeting and gets called out by his intimidating boss.
jokes.punchline: Instead of being reprimanded, Doug approves — 'I like funny' — and enthusiastically welcomes Chandler to the team, subverting the expected punishment.
jokes.explanation: Functional character setup for Doug and the workplace dynamic. The subversion (boss approves of wisecrack) is mildly amusing but not exceptional. It does good expository work establishing Doug's personality.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We are not talking about the stew.

jokes.text: Chandler makes a restaurant reservation under the name 'Winona Ryder' and is delighted when it works.
jokes.setup: Chandler is on the phone trying to get a restaurant reservation.
jokes.punchline: He uses the name 'Winona Ryder' to score a table for six, and it works — which he celebrates like a personal victory.
jokes.explanation: Mild celebrity name-drop humor that was likely funnier in 1997 when Winona Ryder was at peak fame. The celebration sells it more than the premise. Dated but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, why would we put something smelly on Chandler's butt?

jokes.text: Chandler's boss keeps slapping his butt and acting like it's no big deal. Chandler: 'I didn't do anything. I didn't want to be the guy who has a problem with his boss slapping his bottom.'
jokes.setup: Chandler's boss has been enthusiastically slapping his butt as a sign of camaraderie.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's paralysis — 'I didn't want to be the guy who has a problem with his boss slapping his bottom' — captures the absurdity of workplace power dynamics perfectly.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'the guy who has a problem with his boss slapping his bottom' is characteristically Chandler — overly articulated, socially anxious, and self-aware about his own awkwardness. Good character integration; the cringe is real and relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh God, imagine President Joey. *doing Joey voice* 'The State of the Union is... how you doin'?'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Nuclear codes? He'd use them as a pickup line. 'Hey baby, want to see my missile?'

jokes.text: 'I gotta tell you, I think it's okay to be that guy.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has explained his reluctance to complain about the butt-slapping.
jokes.punchline: Joey, normally the one with poor social judgment, gives the single most sensible response imaginable — delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Economy is the standout here — ten words that perfectly encapsulate the situational absurdity and Joey's character (the dumb one giving the reasonable advice). The understatement does all the heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Bonnie is this woman I knew in the group home. She was really weird - she'd collect her own hair after she brushed it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's disgusting!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, and she'd keep it in a box under her bed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait - Bonnie with the hair box? Oh my God, that's the girl who... that's insane!

jokes.text: 'I would never congratulate Monica on a great stew by, you know, grabbing her boob.'
jokes.setup: The friends are discussing the jock butt-slap as a form of congratulations.
jokes.punchline: Rachel uses the gender-swap comparison — she'd never grab Monica's boob to congratulate her on a stew — to highlight the absurdity of the behavior.
jokes.explanation: A solid observational riff that works through specific image-making ('a great stew' + 'grabbing her boob'). The specificity of 'stew' as the achievement being congratulated is what elevates it slightly above generic.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Hoshi was a paid assassin.

dialogue.speaker: Hoshi
dialogue.line: I was a housepainter.

jokes.text: 'For a really great stew, you'd just stick your head in between them.'
jokes.setup: Rachel says she'd never grab Monica's boob to congratulate her on a stew.
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately escalates — for a REALLY great stew, the celebration would be burying your face in her chest.
jokes.explanation: Joey's escalation is perfectly character-driven — his response is not malicious, just genuinely Joey's calibration of celebration-to-achievement. The logical progression ('grabbing = okay stew, head between = great stew') is absurdly reasonable coming from him. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hoshi
dialogue.line: No sex before the fight. It weakens you.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: What if we just do it like, halfway? You know, like just the top half?

jokes.text: 'Can we please go eat?' / 'What are we getting?' / 'Anything but stew.'
jokes.setup: The stew conversation has taken an uncomfortable turn thanks to Joey.
jokes.punchline: Someone suggests food; 'anything but stew' closes the bit with a dry button.
jokes.explanation: Clean button on the stew bit. 'Anything but stew' is brief and effective as a scene-closer. Not exceptional but does its job well.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's just so depressing. I mean, you see these fallen child stars selling pretzels on the street corner, and you think, 'What happened to you?'

jokes.text: Joey's plan to stop the butt-slapping: rub something that smells bad on your butt so when the boss smacks it, his hand will smell.
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming how Chandler can stop his boss from slapping his butt.
jokes.punchline: Joey's strategy: create a smelly-butt deterrent so the boss's hand smells after smacking.
jokes.explanation: Peak Joey logic — the plan is internally coherent (smelly butt = smelly hand = deterrent) but insane. The absurdity is character-perfect: Joey has reasoned his way to a conclusion that only he could reach. The slow build of explanation adds to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You look different. Did you do something different?

dialogue.speaker: Bonnie
dialogue.line: I'm wearing a bra.

jokes.text: 'Now, what could you rub on your butt that would smell bad?' [Long pause as everyone considers this]
jokes.setup: Joey has outlined his smelly-butt plan and now sincerely asks for suggestions.
jokes.punchline: The pause as everyone — against their better judgment — actually thinks about it. The silence IS the joke.
jokes.explanation: The real laugh here is the pause — everyone involuntarily engaging with the absurd question. The reaction beat sells the joke more than any verbal punchline could. Rewatch value because watching the actors' faces during this beat is presumably excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: She has hair! Oh my God, she has hair! It's long, and it's dark, and it's... it's hair!

jokes.text: 'What if Joey was president?'
jokes.setup: Everyone has been seriously contemplating Joey's absurd smelly-butt strategy.
jokes.punchline: Chandler breaks the silence by voicing the existential horror of Joey's brain being in charge of a country.
jokes.explanation: Six words, perfect economy. Chandler's aside perfectly encapsulates the terror-amusement of watching Joey's logic in action. It's a meta-commentary on the group's dynamic, it's quotable, it lands as a button to the whole smelly-butt sequence, and it's completely Chandler. One of the episode's strongest jokes. Would get a big room laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So your boss just walks around slapping people's butts?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, but only the ones he likes. I got slapped three times yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Three times? What did you do?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I have no idea. But I'm starting to think it's less about favoritism and more about the physics of it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The physics of it?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, like, if he slaps you hard enough, you ricochet into the next person, and then they get slapped too. It's like a domino effect of butt-slapping.

jokes.text: Rachel describing Bonnie as 'average height, medium build, bald.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is describing her friend Bonnie whom she wants to set up with Ross.
jokes.punchline: The description builds to 'bald' as if it's a normal physical descriptor, landing as the comedic anchor of the description.
jokes.explanation: The structure is clean — 'average height, medium build' are setup rhythmically for the punchline descriptor. 'Bald' lands as both funny and oddly matter-of-fact, which is funnier than if Rachel had been embarrassed to say it. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Alright team, I've organized a trust fall exercise. But here's the twist — we're going to bond over our shared hatred of Dartmouth!

dialogue.speaker: Coworker
dialogue.line: Um, why Dartmouth?

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Because they're our rivals! Now, everyone repeat after me: 'We hate Dartmouth!'

dialogue.speaker: Coworker
dialogue.line: We hate Dartmouth!

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Louder! DARTMOUTH IS THE WORST!

dialogue.speaker: Coworker
dialogue.line: DARTMOUTH IS THE WORST!

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Yes! Yes! I can feel the team unity! We are ONE against—

dialogue.speaker: Coworker
dialogue.line: Wait, Doug. My sister goes to Dartmouth.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Oh. Well... I'm sure she's... doing her best.

jokes.text: 'That's fine.' / 'Really?' / 'Ross and the bald girl? Absolutely.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has cautiously asked Rachel if it's okay to set Ross up with Bonnie.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'Ross and the bald girl? Absolutely' — the qualifier 'bald girl' reveals the real reason Rachel thinks this is acceptable: she doesn't perceive Bonnie as a real threat.
jokes.explanation: This joke does double duty — it's funny on the surface and it also plants the seed of Rachel's jealousy that pays off later when Bonnie has hair. The 'bald girl' qualifier as a mark of dismissal is sharp character writing. Rewatch bonus because in retrospect you see Rachel's thinking clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh wow, look at this! The Ultimate Fighting combo meal comes with a free cup!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And it's only $2 more than buying everything separately. That's... that's incredible savings!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A free cup! Do you know what I can do with a free cup? I can drink out of it!

jokes.text: Rachel's exaggerated, overcompensating excitement: 'Great! Okay! Good for you! All right!'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just approved the setup with what sounds like genuine enthusiasm.
jokes.punchline: The enthusiasm escalates to a point that it reads as obviously performative — 'Good for you! All right!' — making her underlying feelings visible.
jokes.explanation: A performance-dependent joke — the comedy is in Jennifer Aniston's delivery of obviously forced enthusiasm. Works better on screen than on page. Functional character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How are you holding up? That was quite a fight.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, the crowd loved it. They were chanting my name, throwing things, telling me to get off their guy...

jokes.text: Pete's trainer interrupts the training session to complain about waiting an hour and a half for computer tech support. Pete: 'Could we concentrate on my training?' Trainer: 'It's just hard when I know I have e-mail I can't get.'
jokes.setup: Pete is being trained by a world-class trainer. The trainer suddenly shifts to a consumer complaint about Pete's company's tech support.
jokes.punchline: The incongruity — elite trainer being distracted from championship prep by his unread email — delivered with genuine grievance.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist incongruity — the mundane (email, tech support wait times) interrupting the epic (training for a brutal fighting championship). The trainer's sincerity makes it funnier. The 'I know I have email I can't get' is a nice human-relatable detail.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: You know, I tried to learn MOSS 2 once. Spent three months studying it.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Failed the certification exam by one point. One point!

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: But I didn't give up. I studied harder, retook it.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Failed again. This time by two points.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Turns out I'm just not a MOSS 2 guy. I'm at peace with that now.

jokes.text: 'And Hoshi here used to be a paid assassin.' / 'A house painter! He used to be a house painter!'
jokes.setup: Pete introduces his trainer Hoshi by saying he 'used to be a paid assassin.'
jokes.punchline: Monica frantically corrects this: 'A house painter!' — either genuinely mishearing Pete or desperately trying to reassure herself.
jokes.explanation: Sharp misdirection with excellent economy. Monica's panicked correction works on two levels — we don't know if she mishears or is in denial — and either interpretation is funny. The emphasis repetition 'A house painter! He used to be a house painter!' sells the desperation perfectly. Strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So Pete's fighting this guy next week who trains by having people hit him in the stomach repeatedly.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's crazy! How is that training?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I guess the idea is to build up tolerance. But I think there's an easier way—just date Monica.

jokes.text: 'No boom-boom before big fight!'
jokes.setup: Monica suggests she and Pete could have 'a little workout of our own' before his fight.
jokes.punchline: Hoshi (the trainer) firmly prohibits sex using the toddler-speak 'no boom-boom before big fight.'
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable. 'Boom-boom' as a euphemism for sex delivered with stern authority by a trainer is absurdly funny. The contrast between the gravity of the prohibition and the infantile language is the joke. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Oh, that's nothing. Last week I drove home from a bar, completely wasted, hit a mailbox, kept going.

jokes.text: 'How about just a boom?'
jokes.setup: Hoshi has declared 'no boom-boom before big fight.'
jokes.punchline: Pete negotiates down to 'just a boom' — treating the prohibition as if it were a literal compound word that could be partially permitted.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy joke. Four words that take the trainer's playful euphemism and apply literal logic to it — negotiating 'boom-boom' down to 'a boom' as if it's a compound noun that can be halved. Clever, surprising, and highly quotable. One of the episode's best constructed jokes. Would get a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Doug, I appreciate the enthusiasm, but when you slap someone on the butt, it's considered inappropriate in the workplace.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Oh, you want me to swear more? Okay! *slaps butt* F*** yeah! *slaps butt* S*** yeah!

jokes.text: 'I just bought a pretzel from one of the kids from Fame. That was depressing.'
jokes.setup: Chandler arrives at the Ultimate Fighting event.
jokes.punchline: He's bought a pretzel from a street vendor who is apparently a failed actor — specifically a former cast member of the TV show Fame — which he delivers as a small, melancholy observation.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, melancholy observational humor in Chandler's voice. 'One of the kids from Fame' selling pretzels is a very specific, very 90s celebrity-culture joke — the bathos of a former entertainment star reduced to street vending. 'That was depressing' is the perfect button — Chandler processes New York's cruelty matter-of-factly.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Look, I appreciate the enthusiasm, but could we maybe keep the physical contact to a minimum? I have a very delicate... posterior.

jokes.text: Ross and friends encounter Bonnie — she now has a full head of hair. Ross's double-take: 'This is Bonnie? This is Bonnie? You're Bonnie?'
jokes.setup: Ross agreed to date the 'bald girl' Bonnie; everyone shows up and finds a conventionally attractive woman with full hair.
jokes.punchline: Ross's stunned triple-repetition 'This is Bonnie? This is Bonnie? You're Bonnie?' captures disbelief that crosses from shock to excitement.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the bald girl setup. Works because we've been primed to expect someone bald, and the reveal is Ross (and the audience's) surprise. The triple-repeat structure captures genuine male dumbstruck reaction — repetition as a form of comedic disbelief.

jokes.text: 'I just started wearing bras again.' / 'Oh, that must be it.'
jokes.setup: Ross points out that Bonnie looks very different from when he last saw her — expecting hair to be the obvious answer.
jokes.punchline: Bonnie explains she's just started wearing bras again; Ross accepts this as a plausible explanation with 'Oh, that must be it' — completely sidestepping the obvious (the hair).
jokes.explanation: Strong misdirection — we expect the hair to be addressed, but Bonnie pivots to bras, and Ross plays along as if that satisfies the mystery entirely. The non-sequitur works because both are ignoring the obvious elephant. Economy is excellent — five words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, she's touching his thigh. I mean, that's like, second base.

jokes.text: 'Oh, that must be it.' — Rachel's hollow, stunned response to Bonnie's bra explanation.
jokes.setup: Bonnie credits her new appearance to wearing bras again, not hair
jokes.punchline: Rachel, completely blindsided and internally panicking, can only manage a hollow 'Oh, that must be it' — pretending to accept an absurd explanation while visibly falling apart
jokes.explanation: Rachel's reaction is the real punch — the hollow agreement while processing a crisis is perfectly Courteney Cox-levels of face acting. Economy of the line is excellent: four words, massive subtext.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He's dating Bonnie? Bonnie?! The bald woman?!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She's not completely bald, Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, when he's done with her, I have a very specific demand: his next girlfriend has to be bald. I want him to know what it feels like!

jokes.text: 'You said she was bald.' / 'She was bald. She's not now.' / 'How could you not tell me she has hair?' / 'I don't know. I hardly ever say that about people.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is furious that Phoebe didn't warn her Bonnie grew her hair back.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's defense: 'I hardly ever say that about people' — pointing out that announcing someone has hair is not a normal thing to do, making Rachel's expectation the absurd one.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Phoebe's logic is impeccable and revealing: of course she didn't mention Bonnie has hair now, because people don't go around reporting that their friends have hair. The joke exposes Rachel's jealousy as the irrational force it is, through Phoebe's oblivious but completely correct reasoning. 'I hardly ever say that about people' is perfect in Phoebe's voice and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we killed them! We killed all the ants!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, they're ants.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: They were working together! They had a little society!

jokes.text: 'That girl has got hair all over her head!'
jokes.setup: Rachel is spiraling about Bonnie having hair.
jokes.punchline: Her complaint escalates to the absurd declaration 'hair ALL OVER her head!' — the exaggeration making the jealousy seem simultaneously petty and unhinged.
jokes.explanation: Quotable in isolation. 'Hair all over her head' as an accusation is delightfully unhinged — the emphasis implies this is somehow excessive, which is the joke. Strong Rachel character comedy; jealousy warping perception into absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be the Ultimate Fighting Champion. I'm gonna be the best fighter in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great, Pete.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm gonna fight anybody. I'll fight you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't think so.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: I'll fight Superman.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Pete, Superman's not real.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: So? I'd still kick his ass. I'd fight a kid.

jokes.text: 'Maybe Ross won't like her personality.' / 'Does she have a bad personality?' / 'Oh, no, Bonnie's the best!'
jokes.setup: Rachel is grasping for reasons the date might fail.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe shoots down the only remaining hope by enthusiastically confirming Bonnie is wonderful — completely oblivious to Rachel's agenda.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's obliviousness working against Rachel's interests is a reliable comedy structure. The enthusiasm of 'Oh, no, Bonnie's the best!' perfectly undercuts Rachel's hope. Good Phoebe character integration — she's incapable of being strategically unhelpful.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Pete, this isn't working. I can't be with someone who gets beaten up for a living. I need stability, a future, someone who'll remember our anniversary!

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Wait, you're breaking up with me because of the fighting?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes! And because you might get brain damage and forget who I am.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Monica, I've taken a lot of hits, but I promise I'll remember you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You say that now, but what about in five years?

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Look, if I forget you, you can just tell me again. It's not like I won't recognize you.

jokes.text: Doug: 'Bing! Read your CompuTek proposal. Real home run.' Then physically evades slapping Chandler's butt after he tries to avoid it: 'Barely got you that time!'
jokes.setup: Chandler has been told the boss keeps slapping his butt; now we see Doug in action, hunting Chandler's bottom.
jokes.punchline: Doug pursues the butt-slap with athletic determination, treating it as a game, and celebrates a near-miss: 'Barely got you that time!'
jokes.explanation: The visual comedy of Doug hunting Chandler's butt in a workplace setting is stronger on screen than on page. 'Barely got you that time!' turns the harassment into a sportsman's pursuit, which is both disturbing and funny. Good escalation of the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: You forgot your briefcase on purpose!

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: You just wanted an excuse to get out of work!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That is not true!

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Oh yeah?

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Well take that!

jokes.text: Coworkers complaining they never get slapped: 'We never get smacked.' / 'That's not true. He smacked you once.' / 'Not on purpose. He ricocheted off you and got me.'
jokes.setup: Chandler's coworkers are envious that he's the boss's favorite based solely on butt-slap frequency.
jokes.punchline: One worker's single slap is dismissed as a 'ricochet' off Chandler — not intentional — making the butt-slap currency even more specific and absurd.
jokes.explanation: The 'ricochet' detail is inspired — the workplace butt-slap has become so formalized that there's now a technical distinction between a deliberate slap and an accidental one. This escalation of the absurd internal logic of the Doug plotline is genuinely creative.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Pete won! Pete actually won the Ultimate Fighting Championship!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, he won?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Pete won the Ultimate Fighting Championship?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well... he fought in it.

jokes.text: 'I'm telling you, I need some smacks.'
jokes.setup: Chandler's coworker is upset at being excluded from the boss's butt-slap favoritism.
jokes.punchline: The coworker expresses genuine deprivation: 'I need some smacks' — treating workplace ass-slapping as a legitimate professional need.
jokes.explanation: Four words that perfectly capture the absurdist logic the episode has built — the butt-slap as professional validation. 'I need some smacks' said with sincerity is a strong payoff line.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: And Bruiser is going for his favorite area.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Aw, that's sweet! He has a favorite area!

jokes.text: Doug: 'I got a kid starting Dartmouth.' Chandler: 'Dartmouth? Who went to Dartmouth? Dartmouth sucks!' [Pause] Doug: 'You go to Dartmouth?' Chandler: 'No, sir.' Doug: 'There you go!'
jokes.setup: Doug mentions his kid is going to Dartmouth; Chandler instinctively trash-talks it to agree with the boss, then panics when he realizes Doug might have gone there.
jokes.punchline: Doug didn't go to Dartmouth and approves of Chandler's dismissal; Chandler's gamble pays off — but only by luck.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe tension — the pause after 'Dartmouth sucks!' while Chandler waits to see if he's torpedoed himself is well-constructed. The relief payoff ('No, sir.' / 'There you go!') is satisfying. Chandler's boss-pleasing anxiety is very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, that's not good for his sperm count.

jokes.text: 'God, Ross! What is that?' / 'The Ultimate Fighting Combo. I saved 30 cents. Plus, I get to keep the cup.'
jokes.setup: Ross has arrived at the Ultimate Fighting event with an enormous combo meal.
jokes.punchline: Ross defends his giant food purchase with two specific justifications — the savings and the cup — that together paint a perfect picture of his practical-nerd enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Strong Ross characterization — the specificity of '30 cents' and 'I get to keep the cup' is very him. The two-part justification lands because of the cup detail, which is both relatable and pathetic in a lovable way. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Tank Abbott is announced as Pete's opponent: '300-pound street fighter from Huntington Beach, California.'
jokes.setup: Pete's been introduced as a tech billionaire making his debut fight.
jokes.punchline: His opponent is a 300-pound professional street fighter — the mismatch itself is the joke before a punch has been thrown.
jokes.explanation: The mismatch is funny conceptually and works as a visual setup for the beating to come. Not a joke in itself so much as context-comedy — the absurdity of the pairing is the humor.

jokes.text: 'I'll use his strength and weight against him.' / 'Well, then that guy is in serious, serious trouble.'
jokes.setup: Pete reassures Monica by explaining his martial arts strategy for fighting the 300-pound Tank Abbott.
jokes.punchline: Joey earnestly agrees that Tank Abbott is in trouble — completely believing Pete's delusional confidence.
jokes.explanation: Joey's gullibility playing straight to Pete's delusion is a reliable comedy structure. 'Serious, serious trouble' repeated for emphasis is a nice touch — Joey being emphatically wrong. Character integration is solid.

jokes.text: Pete regains consciousness after the fight. Monica says 'It's me. Monica.' / Pete: 'Who else would it be?' / Monica: 'Earlier, when you were coming to, you called me Fran.'
jokes.setup: Pete has been knocked out; Monica identifies herself to the disoriented Pete.
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals he called her 'Fran' when he was coming to — implying there's a Fran in Pete's life he was thinking of while semi-conscious.
jokes.explanation: A quick comedic beat that adds a layer to Pete's character while he's at his most vulnerable. The 'Fran' detail is funny because it's specific enough to feel real. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'It would be nice after hearing 20,000 people chant, "You suck!"'
jokes.setup: Monica says she's proud of Pete for doing the fight.
jokes.punchline: Pete's response — that a compliment would be nice given he just heard 20,000 people chant that he sucks — delivered with understated pathos.
jokes.explanation: Dark understatement works here — the scale of the public humiliation (20,000 people) versus the mild need for a private compliment creates a nice comedic gap. The specificity of '20,000' elevates it above a generic bad-day joke.

jokes.text: Pete explains his persistence by citing MOSS 865: 'MOSS 1 burned down my dad's garage. MOSS 2 would only schedule appointments in January. And 862 others that I learned from.'
jokes.setup: Pete uses his software development history to explain why he won't quit Ultimate Fighting after one brutal loss.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that there were 864 failed versions before success, with the specific absurd failures (burned the garage, only schedules January appointments) escalating the comedy.
jokes.explanation: Pete's tech-entrepreneur logic applied to getting beaten up is good character comedy. The specific details ('burned down my dad's garage,' 'only schedule appointments in January') are excellently chosen — they escalate from catastrophic to absurdly specific. Good escalation structure.

jokes.text: 'Just like I learned from this fight — never to let a guy stand on my neck.' / 'You didn't know that already?'
jokes.setup: Pete is drawing a lesson from his humiliating defeat, building toward some martial wisdom.
jokes.punchline: The lesson is simply 'never let a guy stand on your neck' — and Monica's astonished 'You didn't know that already?' punctures any pretension.
jokes.explanation: Strong structure — Pete frames his lesson with the weight of MOSS 865's wisdom, then the lesson itself is something any person would consider obvious. Monica's 'You didn't know that already?' is perfectly economical and the best she gets this episode. The joke earns its laugh through the contrast between the solemn framing and the banal content.

jokes.text: Pete reveals Hoshi thinks Monica being ringside affected his concentration. Monica: 'Yeah. That was the problem.'
jokes.setup: Pete gently suggests that Monica's presence at ringside — not the 300-pound street fighter — was what caused him to lose.
jokes.punchline: Monica's dry 'Yeah. That was the problem' — accepting the absurd excuse with barely concealed sarcasm.
jokes.explanation: Monica's sarcasm is earned and the economy is good — she doesn't over-explain the absurdity, just lets 'Yeah. That was the problem' do the work. The joke lands on the gap between Pete's delusional reasoning and reality.

jokes.text: Opponent trains by going to Iran and pulling the arms off thieves.
jokes.setup: Friends are watching the TV coverage before Pete's next fight.
jokes.punchline: The training regime described — going to Iran to pull the arms off thieves — is presented as a factual sports fact, casually delivered.
jokes.explanation: Good dark absurdism — the specificity of 'Iran' and 'pulling the arms off thieves' as a reported training method is both horrifying and funny because it's delivered as sports commentary. The casualness of the delivery is key.

jokes.text: 'Hot dog? Four, please.'
jokes.setup: The group is nervously anticipating Pete's fight and discussing how anxious they are.
jokes.punchline: Joey hears 'hot dog' and immediately orders four — his appetite completely unaffected by the tension.
jokes.explanation: Short, sharp, character-perfect. Joey ordering four hot dogs in the middle of someone else's emotional tension is quintessential Joey — food always wins. The 'four' is the key detail; one would be normal, four is the joke. Very strong character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I gotta tell you, I wasn't expecting to like her at all.' Then, after pausing: 'I actually wasn't expecting to like anyone right now. But she's really terrific.' Others respond: 'It's too bad.' / 'There are other fish in the sea.'
jokes.setup: Ross is saying he liked Bonnie; Rachel and Phoebe respond as if he's expressing sadness.
jokes.punchline: Despite Ross clearly saying he liked Bonnie, Rachel and Phoebe respond with condolences — 'It's too bad,' 'There are other fish in the sea' — revealing their desire for the date to have failed.
jokes.explanation: Good irony structure — the gap between what Ross is saying and what Rachel/Phoebe are hearing (or pretending to hear) is the joke. Their 'other fish in the sea' while he's saying he liked her is excellent character-driven irony.

jokes.text: 'Oh, I gotta tell you, I wasn't expecting to like her at all.' / 'It's too bad.' / 'No, I'm saying I liked her.' / 'There are other fish in the sea.' / 'I think she's great, okay? We're going out again.' / 'I hear you. Are you capable of talking about anything else?'
jokes.setup: Ross tries to share good news about his date with Bonnie
jokes.punchline: Rachel is in such denial that she keeps mistranslating Ross's positive statements as negative ones, even correcting herself with more denial — until she snaps with 'are you capable of talking about anything else?'
jokes.explanation: Extended character comedy that works because the escalation of denial is carefully structured. Rachel actively mishears good news as bad, which reveals the depth of her jealousy while being genuinely funny. The final snap ('are you capable of talking about anything else?') is a great button since she's the one who can't stop thinking about it.

jokes.text: 'Which one's my turkey burger?' / 'The one next to my foot. Sorry.'
jokes.setup: The friends are eating at the fight event.
jokes.punchline: Someone's food has ended up next to someone's foot — a casual, gross admission delivered without any drama.
jokes.explanation: Mild gross-out sight gag that works on minimal craft. The 'sorry' without any attempt to rectify the situation is the small comedic beat. Functional but the weakest food joke of the episode.

jokes.text: Chandler reports his boss tried to slap him nine times in one day. 'I had to put on lotion.'
jokes.setup: Joey asks if the boss tried to slap Chandler again.
jokes.punchline: Nine times in a day — escalation from 'some slapping' to a frequency requiring lotion application.
jokes.explanation: The lotion detail is inspired — it implies sufficient frequency that Chandler had to adapt, which is funnier than just saying 'a lot.' Nine is a good specific number (not ten, which would feel round and fake). Strong running gag escalation.

jokes.text: Chandler tells Doug he didn't do his work: 'Instead, I hung out with some friends and had a couple of beers. So I certainly don't deserve praise. Verbal... or otherwise.'
jokes.setup: Chandler confronts Doug about the butt-slapping by confessing he didn't do his work.
jokes.punchline: 'So I certainly don't deserve praise — verbal, or otherwise.' The pause before 'or otherwise' is Chandler flagging the butt-slap without saying it.
jokes.explanation: Very Chandler — the elaborate verbal setup to avoid saying 'stop slapping my butt' directly. 'Verbal... or otherwise' is perfectly constructed with the pause doing comedic work. Strong character integration; only Chandler would approach this confrontation this way.

jokes.text: 'So I certainly don't deserve praise. Verbal...or otherwise.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just confessed he didn't do the assigned work and wants to pre-emptively foreclose the butt-slap
jokes.punchline: 'Or otherwise' — the delayed tag that specifically refers to the butt-slap without naming it, treating the slap as a known category of praise
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The pause before 'or otherwise' is doing tremendous work — it's the most precise possible reference to butt-slapping without saying it. The euphemism creates a shared understanding between Chandler and the audience while flying slightly over Doug's head. Chandler's awkward delicacy here is peak character comedy.

jokes.text: Doug: 'I got tanked myself last night. Pretty dicey drive home. Tappan Zee Bridge never looked smaller.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has confessed to getting drunk with friends instead of doing work.
jokes.punchline: Doug one-ups him by casually admitting to drunk driving over the Tappan Zee Bridge — delivered as relatable camaraderie.
jokes.explanation: Doug as a character is elevated by his casual criminality — drunk driving offered as a bonding moment. 'Tappan Zee Bridge never looked smaller' is a vivid, darkly funny image. Good dark character comedy that makes Doug both funnier and more disturbing.

jokes.text: 'That's okay. You're still my number-one guy! Bing!' — followed by an enthusiastic butt-slap.
jokes.setup: Chandler just confessed to not doing his work specifically to avoid praise
jokes.punchline: Doug slaps him anyway — the ultimate running-gag payoff where the planned deterrent completely fails
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff — Chandler's entire plan to avoid praise backfired, and Doug is constitutionally incapable of withholding his enthusiasm. The running gag structure is earning its dividends here.

jokes.text: Chandler confronts Doug about the butt-slapping: 'I'm a little bit uncomfortable with the way that you express yourself.' / Doug: 'Is it the swearing? Because you can just kiss my ass!'
jokes.setup: Chandler carefully begins raising his discomfort with Doug's behavior.
jokes.punchline: Doug immediately assumes it's the swearing and tells Chandler to 'kiss my ass' — obliviously using a butt reference while Chandler is trying to talk about his butt.
jokes.explanation: Excellent ironic structure — Doug's attempt to demonstrate he's not offensive uses the phrase 'kiss my ass,' which is both a butt reference and an ironic intensification of the exact problem Chandler is raising. The layers work: verbal irony + physical irony + character comedy all in one exchange. Well-earned.

jokes.text: Chandler explains the problem is the way Doug 'concentrate[s] his enthusiasm... on my buttocks.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to diplomatically explain the butt-slapping to Doug.
jokes.punchline: 'Concentrate your enthusiasm on my buttocks' — Chandler's signature euphemistic over-articulation applied to a problem that could be stated in five words.
jokes.explanation: Peak Chandler verbal style — taking something direct and making it maximally circuitous. 'Concentrate your enthusiasm on my buttocks' is an impeccable Chandler-ism: formal register applied to physical comedy. 9.0 on character integration because this phrasing belongs exclusively to this character.

jokes.text: 'And besides, it's making all the other guys jealous.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is listing reasons why the butt-slapping is problematic.
jokes.punchline: His final argument is that the other employees are jealous of the slaps — incorporating the absurd coworker subplot as a real negotiating point.
jokes.explanation: Smart callback — Chandler uses the coworkers' jealousy (established in #40-41) as a legitimate workplace concern to present to his boss. The joke works because it treats the absurd as real: the jealousy over butt-slaps is being raised as an HR issue. Strong structural payoff to an earlier bit.

jokes.text: Doug responds: 'It takes guts to bring this up. Bing, you're okay.' Then slaps his own butt in celebration.
jokes.setup: Doug has received Chandler's complaint with surprising grace.
jokes.punchline: Doug celebrates Chandler's bravery by slapping — his own butt. Implicitly ending the external slapping by internalizing it.
jokes.explanation: This is the best payoff of the butt-slapping arc. Doug solves the complaint by transferring the slapping to himself — it's unexpected, perfectly logical within his character, and visually very funny. The internal consistency (he still needs to slap a butt; it just has to be his own) makes this both a great button and a great character moment. High impact, strong structure.

jokes.text: 'Would you rather live in the shirt pocket of a sweaty giant or inside his shower drain?'
jokes.setup: No explicit setup — Joey randomly poses a hypothetical.
jokes.punchline: The hypothetical is both vivid and grotesque — sweaty shirt pocket vs. shower drain — delivered as if it's a normal thought to have.
jokes.explanation: A classic Joey 'would you rather' absurdism. The specificity is good (sweaty giant, shower drain) and it comes from nowhere, which is very Joey. Both options are unpleasant in specific ways, which is the design of a good would-you-rather. 8.0 character integration — this is a distinctly Joey activity.

jokes.text: 'Oh my God. Look. It's Ross and that girl.' [They spy Ross and Bonnie through a window]
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe catch sight of Ross and Bonnie outside, apparently on their date.
jokes.punchline: The sudden shift from Joey's absurd hypothetical to Rachel panicking at the sight of Ross with Bonnie is a sharp tonal juxtaposition.
jokes.explanation: Scene transition joke — the humor is partially in the abruptness of Rachel's distress interrupting Joey's hypothetical. Functional but not strong on its own.

jokes.text: 'Look. It's a line of ants! They're working as a team!'
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe are obsessively watching Ross and Bonnie through the window.
jokes.punchline: Joey is completely uninterested in the Ross-Bonnie drama and has instead become fascinated by a line of ants nearby.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey moment — while everyone is emotionally invested in the relationship drama, Joey's attention is captured by ants. 'They're working as a team!' is delivered with the same genuine awe Joey brings to his hot dog orders. Excellent character integration — the ants are more interesting to Joey than human drama, which tells you everything about him.

jokes.text: 'Right. Oh, yeah. It looks like Ross is breaking up with her.' / 'I hope he lets her down easy.' / 'Look at that! They are not breaking up! Look at them!'
jokes.setup: Rachel is watching Ross and Bonnie through the window, catastrophizing
jokes.punchline: Rachel first misreads the situation as a breakup (what she wants), then is horrified to see it's actually going well — her wishful misinterpretation immediately corrected by reality
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Rachel's wishful thinking immediately demolished by reality is a reliable comedic structure. Works well in the scene context.

jokes.text: Rachel and Phoebe observe Ross and Bonnie through the window: 'It looks like Ross is breaking up with her.' / 'I hope he lets her down easy.' / 'They are NOT breaking up! Look at them! That's a second date, that's what that is!'
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe are window-watching Ross and Bonnie's date, narrating what they see.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's momentary hope that they're breaking up is immediately crushed when the evidence clearly shows a romantic second date, and she spirals.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy showing Rachel's jealousy escalating in real time. The quick reversal from 'breaking up' to 'SECOND DATE' captures her spiral well. The comedy lives in Rachel's self-delusion being punctured by reality.

jokes.text: 'She just put her hand on his thigh.' / 'That's nothing. She's very sexually aggressive.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe reports what she sees on the date.
jokes.punchline: Rachel dismisses the thigh touch by explaining it as Bonnie just being 'very sexually aggressive' — which is not the reassurance it appears to be.
jokes.explanation: Rachel's attempt to minimize ('that's nothing') is undercut by the explanation ('she's very sexually aggressive') which is actually worse. Good ironic self-defeating logic.

jokes.text: 'It's your fault. Now he loves her. He'll marry her. It's all your fault.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is blaming Phoebe for setting up Ross with Bonnie.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's catastrophizing rockets from 'he likes her' to 'he loves her, he'll marry her' in seconds — the speed of escalation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Rachel's catastrophizing arc is a reliable character comedy beat. The acceleration from date to marriage in one breath is funny because it mirrors how jealousy actually works. Good character integration.

jokes.text: 'We have to break them up. Just go in there and shave her head! You owe me one bald girl!'
jokes.setup: Rachel demands Phoebe do something about Ross and Bonnie.
jokes.punchline: 'You owe me one bald girl!' — the logical conclusion of Rachel's bald-girl logic: restore Bonnie to her original non-threatening state.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'You owe me one bald girl' is perfectly constructed — the logic of Rachel's jealousy taken to its absurd endpoint (literally de-hairing the competition), delivered with complete conviction. It's highly quotable, character-perfect, and the 'one bald girl' phrasing treats a human being as a commodity in the most hilariously petty way possible. Great callback payoff to the entire bald arc.

jokes.text: Phoebe asks the obvious: 'Aren't you the one that decided you didn't want to be with Ross? ... Well, isn't he your friend? Don't you want him to be happy?' / Rachel: 'Yes.' [Long pause] / 'So?' [Longer pause] / 'It's just, I didn't expect him to be this happy so soon.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls out Rachel's hypocrisy — she broke up with Ross and said she wanted him to be happy.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's answers get slower and softer until she lands on 'I didn't expect him to be this happy so soon' — a painfully honest and funny admission.
jokes.explanation: The comedic value here is in the pauses — Rachel knows she's wrong, and the increasing silence between Phoebe's questions and her answers IS the joke. 'So?' / [long pause] / 'It's just...' is a very human admission that's funny because it's so recognizable. The rewatch bonus is in watching Phoebe's dawning realization.

jokes.text: 'It's just, you know, I didn't expect him to be this happy so soon.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has been caught unable to say she wants Ross to be happy
jokes.punchline: Her honest admission — 'I didn't expect him to be this happy so soon' — is the painfully relatable confession behind all of her jealous scheming
jokes.explanation: This is the comedic truth-reveal — the joke beneath all the scheming. 'So soon' is the perfect specific grievance: she'd be fine with him being happy eventually, just not already. Highly relatable and quotable.

jokes.text: 'Oh, no. What?' / 'We killed them all!' [The ants]
jokes.setup: Joey was enchanted by the ant line earlier.
jokes.punchline: Cut to Joey discovering the ants are dead — his devastation is entirely sincere and completely disproportionate to the situation.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff to the ants joke. Joey's horror at the ants' demise — 'we killed them all!' — is perfect because his emotional investment in the ants was established earlier and his grief is completely sincere. The juxtaposition with the Rachel/Phoebe drama resolving is a nice structural counterpoint. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'It's not as bad as it looks. It's a precaution. I'm not supposed to move my spine.'
jokes.setup: Monica visits Pete after a second brutal fight; he's visibly in a terrible state.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not supposed to move my spine' — delivered as a minor inconvenience rather than the catastrophic medical crisis it is.
jokes.explanation: Good dark understatement — 'I'm not supposed to move my spine' as a breezy aside is funny precisely because of the scale of injury being minimized. Pete's cheerfulness about catastrophic injury is consistent character comedy.

jokes.text: Pete describes his future legacy: 'The day will come when children will argue over who would win a fight — me or Superman.' / 'Not that I could beat Superman, but kids are stupid.'
jokes.setup: Pete is articulating his grand vision — children arguing about his fighting prowess.
jokes.punchline: The immediate qualification — 'not that I could beat Superman, but kids are stupid' — undercuts the grandiose vision while maintaining Pete's earnest delusion.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed jokes. The structure is almost perfect — grandiose delusion (children debating him vs. Superman) immediately self-corrected ('not that I could beat Superman'), then salvaged by complete contempt for children ('kids are stupid'). Three beats, none wasted, and the self-awareness makes Pete simultaneously more ridiculous and more charming. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Monica catalogues Pete's injuries: 'A torn rotator cuff, a hairline fracture in my right forearm, a severely bruised Adam's apple...' Pete: 'But that really hurt.'
jokes.setup: Monica is listing Pete's injuries to convince him to stop fighting.
jokes.punchline: Pete adds 'but that really hurt' about the Adam's apple — his pain hierarchy suggesting that spinal restrictions and fractures are merely inconvenient, but the Adam's apple was the genuine suffering.
jokes.explanation: The comedic logic of Pete's pain hierarchy is funny — fracture and rotator cuff are apparently manageable, but the Adam's apple is where he draws the line of genuine suffering. The specific body part (Adam's apple) adds to the absurdity.

jokes.text: 'You are terrible at this, okay? You are the worst ultimate fighter ever. Ever!'
jokes.setup: Monica has reached her limit with Pete's refusal to quit
jokes.punchline: Monica's competitive-person-telling-someone-they're-the-worst, with the double 'Ever! Ever!' — the emphatic repetition undermining any softness
jokes.explanation: Monica's competitive honesty coming out in a moment of emotional vulnerability is good character work. 'Ever. Ever.' has good comedic rhythm.

jokes.text: 'Monica? Could you leave a note? I'm on painkillers and I might not remember this tomorrow.'
jokes.setup: Monica has just broken up with Pete in an emotional scene.
jokes.punchline: Pete, clearly heavily medicated, asks Monica to leave a note summarizing their breakup because he might not remember it.
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. The ask is perfectly constructed — after a sincere emotional breakup scene, Pete punctures the pathos with a completely reasonable (within his circumstances) request. The joke works because it's character-true: Pete is on painkillers, Pete is practical (he's a tech billionaire who built MOSS 865), and the idea of getting a written summary of your own breakup is both tragic and absurd. Economy is excellent: 'I might not remember this tomorrow' is the perfect closing beat. High quotability, rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Doug's meeting wrap-up: 'Lines all go up, so I'm happy.' Then proceeds to individually compliment each staff member with escalating energy, including 'Goldberg, you maniac!'
jokes.setup: Chandler's confrontation with Doug seemed to resolve things — now back in a team meeting
jokes.punchline: Doug's management style is unchanged — same chaotic energy, same random enthusiasm — 'Goldberg, you maniac!' as a professional compliment
jokes.explanation: 'Goldberg, you maniac!' as workplace praise is a funny Doug-specific character beat. His anarchic management style has its own internal logic that's consistently amusing.

jokes.text: Chandler 'forgot his briefcase by accident' to return to the office. Doug: 'Forgot something else too, you bastard!' Then slaps Chandler's butt anyway.
jokes.setup: Chandler has supposedly resolved the butt-slapping issue with Doug earlier.
jokes.punchline: Doug cannot help himself — he slaps Chandler's butt one more time, framing it as a happy accident with 'you bastard!' suggesting Doug knew he would relapse.
jokes.explanation: Good character callback — Doug's resolution was temporary and he inevitably reverts. The 'forgot something else too, you bastard!' implies Doug knows this about himself. The running gag gets one more bump before the episode ends.

jokes.text: 'I forgot my briefcase, you know, by accident.' / 'Of course you did. Forgot something else too, you bastard!'
jokes.setup: Chandler had his formal conversation with Doug and thought things were resolved
jokes.punchline: Doug returns, calls Chandler a 'bastard' with affection — and presumably slaps him again, showing the conversation changed nothing about his fundamental behavior
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff — Doug's conversation with Chandler changed nothing, which is both the joke and the character revelation. 'By accident' as a fake-out of why he returned is a slight misdirection.

jokes.text: Fight commentary: 'Bruiser is charging! Run. Run, you crazy, rich freak!'
jokes.setup: The friends are watching Pete's fight on TV.
jokes.punchline: Joey's commentary collapses from sports commentary style to direct audience pleading — 'Run, you crazy, rich freak!' — which is both accurate and affectionate.
jokes.explanation: 'Crazy, rich freak' as a term of endearment for Pete is perfectly Joey — accurate, affectionate, and completely unselfconscious. The shift from sports commentary to direct plea is funny.

jokes.text: 'Check it out! Pete's winning!' / 'Really?' / 'No!'
jokes.setup: Monica can't bear to watch Pete's fight.
jokes.punchline: Joey gets Monica's hopes up with 'Pete's winning!' then immediately crushes them with 'No!' — the speed of the reversal is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the entire joke lives in the 'No!' being delivered as fast as possible after Monica's 'Really?' The structure is simple but impeccably timed on the page. High economy score for three words doing maximum work.

jokes.text: Commentary: 'Bruiser has Becker on the canvas and is going for his favorite area!'
jokes.setup: Fight commentary describes Bruiser targeting a specific area.
jokes.punchline: 'His favorite area' — the ominous vagueness of which body part Bruiser prefers to attack is the setup for the following joke.
jokes.explanation: Setup joke — its value is primarily in establishing the punchline that follows. Works in context, weak in isolation.

jokes.text: 'Wait! If that's his favorite area, why is he being so mean to it?'
jokes.setup: The announcer has said Bruiser is 'going for his favorite area' (presumably the groin).
jokes.punchline: Phoebe takes 'favorite area' completely literally — if you love something, why would you hurt it? Her logic is internally consistent and completely misses the point.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Phoebe joke — the logic is impeccably Phoebe, applying literal interpretive charity to an announcer's euphemism. 'If that's his favorite area, why is he being so mean to it?' is both genuinely funny and completely in character. High character integration; only Phoebe asks this question. Strong economy.

jokes.text: 'This is ironic. Your last boyfriend, Richard, didn't want to have kids. From the looks of it, now Pete can't.'
jokes.setup: Bruiser is attacking Pete's groin area.
jokes.punchline: Chandler draws the parallel between Richard not wanting kids and Pete now being physically unable to have them — delivered as an observation about Monica's romantic pattern.
jokes.explanation: Sharp series callback and dark comedy that works on multiple levels: it's a real character observation (Monica's bad luck with fertility in relationships), it's timed perfectly at the darkest moment of the fight, and it shows Chandler's wit at its best — finding an elegant pattern in pain. 'Didn't want to have kids / now Pete can't' is a clean parallel structure. One of Chandler's best lines of the episode.

tmdb_overview: To Monica's horror, Pete wants to be the Ultimate Fighting Champion. Chandler has a problem when his new boss is slaphappy. Phoebe sets Ross up on a date with a woman who used to be bald. The group overhears a scandalous conversation at Central Perk.
insight: Mid-tier escalation comedy undercuts character moments in this season finale.
